procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The complainant filed a revision petition under Section 397 read with Section 401 Cr.P.C. before the High Court being Criminal Revision Case No. 628 of 2016. The High Court allowed the revision petition and directed the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate to summon the appellants herein and to face the trial in the said case. The High Court of Judicature at Madras dismissed the Civil Revision Petition on October 25, 2007.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellants approached the Supreme Court by way of Criminal Appeal No. 1720 of 2017, challenging the High Court's order dated 01.06.2017 in Criminal Revision Case No. 628 of 2016. The tenant/de facto complainant preferred a Special Leave Petition before this Court against the order dated October 25, 2007, but was unsuccessful in getting stay order as his special leave petition was also dismissed by this Court on April 07, 2008.

issue.issue_text: The degree of satisfaction that is required for invoking the powers under Section 319 CrPC and the related question is as to in what situations this power should be exercised in respect of a person named in the FIR but not charge-sheeted.

facts: The provided text does not contain specific facts of the case. It focuses on the legal principles governing the issue.

law.law_text: The power under Section 319 of the Criminal Procedure Code (CrPC) is a discretionary and extraordinary power that must be exercised sparingly.
The power can be invoked against a person not named as an accused in the charge sheet if it appears from the evidence presented during the trial that they have committed an offence.
The standard for invoking this power is a degree of satisfaction that is "much stricter" than the prima facie case required for framing a charge.

The test to be applied is one which is "more than prima facie case as exercised at the time of framing of charge, but short of satisfaction to an extent that the evidence, if goes unrebutted, would lead to conviction."
The power should only be exercised when "strong and cogent evidence" emerges against a person from the evidence led before the court during the trial.

The evidence for invoking Section 319 must be that which is recorded in court during the trial. Material collected by the investigating officer can be used for corroboration but is not the primary basis for invoking the power.

application.application_text: The Supreme Court addressed the first part of the issue—the required degree of satisfaction—by citing the Constitution Bench decision in the *Hardeep Singh* case. It clarified that while the test is one of a prima facie case, the standard is significantly higher than that used for framing charges against an accused.

The Court established a specific two-pronged test for this satisfaction: the evidence must be stronger than that needed to frame a charge, but it does not need to be so conclusive that it would guarantee a conviction if left unchallenged.

Regarding the second part of the issue—when to exercise this power for a person named in the FIR but not charge-sheeted—the Court explained that the power under Section 319 is specifically meant for such situations. Even if the police have not implicated a person, the court is not powerless.

However, the Court specified that this power is triggered only when "strong and cogent evidence" against such a person "surfaces during the trial" from the evidence led before the court. It cannot be exercised casually or based merely on the initial investigation material that the police had already considered.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court, relying on the principles laid down in the *Hardeep Singh* case, decided that the power under Section 319 CrPC can be invoked against a person named in the FIR but not charge-sheeted only when strong and cogent evidence emerges against them during the trial. The degree of satisfaction required is more than a prima facie case for framing charges but falls short of the level of proof required for a conviction.

issue.issue_text: Whether the delinquent's charges have been proved or not?

facts: A departmental inquiry was conducted against the appellant/bailiff on two charges.
The first charge was for dereliction of duty for not following the correct procedure under Order XXI Rule 35 of the Code of Civil Procedure when executing a warrant.
The second charge was for using 50-60 rowdy persons to ransack the complainant's premises, which was the same allegation as in the criminal FIR.
The Inquiry Officer found that the first charge of dereliction of duty had been proved.
However, the Inquiry Officer found that the second, more serious charge was not proved.
application: The Court noted that the Inquiry Officer's report concluded that the second charge was not proved because the complainant was not an eyewitness to the alleged incident.
Additionally, two other witnesses examined during the inquiry had not spoken about any illegal activities committed by the bailiff.
The Court also observed that in the separate criminal proceedings, there was no specific attribution against the bailiff in the FIR or in the depositions of the prosecution witnesses (PWs 1 to 6).
The police investigation following the FIR also did not find anything against the bailiff.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court determined that the serious charges against the bailiff had not been proved. The only charge that was established, and only in the departmental inquiry, was for dereliction of duty, not the criminal allegations of using rowdy elements and ransacking the property.

arguments.issue_text: The degree of satisfaction that is required for invoking the powers under Section 319 CrPC and the related question is as to in what situations this power should be exercised in respect of a person named in the FIR but not charge-sheeted.
appellant_arguments: The application to summon the appellants under Section 319 Cr.P.C. was a belated afterthought, filed long after the complainant (PW-1) had testified and after the prosecution had already closed its evidence.
There is insufficient 'evidence' to meet the standard required for Section 319 Cr.P.C.
The complainant (PW-1) and other witnesses (PWs 2, 3, and 4) did not testify about any conspiracy involving the appellants.
The appellants (landlords) were not present at the scene of the crime.
A comprehensive police investigation found no involvement of the appellants, which is why they were not included in the charge sheet.
The complainant did not file a protest petition when the charge sheet was submitted without naming the appellants.
The High Court was wrongly influenced by the mere mention of the appellants' names in the FIR and the complainant's deposition.
One of the appellants, the bailiff, was only discharging his official duties and was found to have done so by the police investigation.
respondent_arguments: Sufficient material exists in the testimony of prosecution witnesses (PW1 to PW6) to show that the appellants were the perpetrators of the offence.
The criminal acts were committed at the behest and for the benefit of the appellants.
After the premises were ransacked, the stolen goods were taken to the appellants' premises.
Based on the evidence, the appellants should be made to face trial.
The High Court's decision to summon the appellants is in accordance with settled principles of law and should not be interfered with.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The aforesaid reasons given by the High Court do not stand the judicial scrutiny. The High Court has not dealt with the subject matter properly and even in the absence of strong and cogent evidence against the appellant, it has set aside the order of the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate and exercised its discretion in summoning in summoning the appellants as accused persons.
legal_tests_applied: The power under Section 319 CrPC should be exercised 'only where strong and cogent evidence occurs against a person from the evidence led before the court that such power should be exercised and not in a casual and cavalier manner.'
why_appellant_lost: The appellants/landlords were admittedly not present at the site when the alleged incident took place, there is no 'evidence' within the meaning of s.319 C1:P.C. on the basis of which they could be summoned as accused persons.
The Police had, after thorough investigation, filed the charge sheet in which the appellants were not implicated, however. the complainant had not filed any protest petition at that stage.
As regards the appellant-bailiff, there was no specific attribution in the FIR or in the depositions of PWs 1 to 6 in the Court.

The Police, during investigation, after the registration of FIR, did not find anything against the appellant/bailiff and even the department did not find anything against him in the departmental inquiry.
During trial, no 'strong and cogent evidence' has surfaced against the appellant/bailiff on the basis of which he could be summoned.
policy_considerations: The court is sole repository of justice and a duty is cast upon it to uphold the rule oflaw and, therefore, it will be inappropriate to deny the existence of such powers with the courts in our criminal justice system where it is not uncommon that the real accused, at times, get away by manipulating the investigating and/or the prosecuting agency.
